subject: Chemistry
title: Why Ice Floats
description: A quick, practical guide to Why Ice Floats.

hook.text: Almost every substance sinks when it freezes. Water does the opposite—ice floats. This is bizarre.

buildup.text: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds. In liquid water, these bonds constantly break and reform.

discovery.text: When water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock into a rigid hexagonal structure with gaps. Ice is less dense than liquid water.

twist.text: If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up, killing all aquatic life. Floating ice insulates the water below.

climax.text: This single chemical quirk may be why life exists on Earth. Liquid water survives under floating ice.

punchline.text: Hydrogen bonds make ice float. That accident may have saved all life.

quiz.question: Why does ice float on water?
options: Hydrogen bonds create a rigid structure with gaps, making ice less dense
Air bubbles trapped in ice make it buoyant
Ice contains less hydrogen than liquid water

details.summary: Ice floats because water expands by about nine percent when it freezes, becoming less dense than liquid water. This anomalous behavior occurs because hydrogen bonds in the ice crystal lattice hold water molecules in an open hexagonal arrangement that takes up more space than the liquid state.
details.whyItMatters: Floating ice insulates lakes and oceans, allowing life to survive beneath frozen surfaces. If ice sank, bodies of water would freeze from the bottom up, devastating aquatic ecosystems.
takeaways: Water is one of very few substances whose solid is less dense than its liquid
Hydrogen bonds create an open hexagonal crystal structure in ice
Floating ice insulates the water below, protecting aquatic life

faq.question: Why does water expand when most substances contract upon freezing?
faq.answer: In liquid water, hydrogen bonds constantly break and reform, allowing molecules to pack relatively closely. When water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock into a rigid hexagonal lattice with large gaps between molecules. This open structure is less dense than the dynamic liquid arrangement.

faq.question: What would happen to life on Earth if ice did not float?
faq.answer: Lakes and oceans would freeze from the bottom up. Without an insulating ice cap, entire bodies of water could freeze solid in winter, killing most aquatic life. Earth's climate and ocean circulation patterns would be fundamentally different, likely making the planet far less hospitable.
